data.name: Juice Shop Angular SPA
data.description: Single-page application built with Angular 17+ and TypeScript that delivers the entire user-facing UI including product catalog, shopping cart, user profile, hacking-instructor overlay, and OAuth login flow. Compiled and served as static assets by the Express backend on port 3000.

threats.title: [F-005] Email-derived password (frontend/src/app/oauth/oauth.component.ts:30)
threats.description:
An attacker who knows any Juice Shop OAuth user's email address computes that account's password offline as btoa(email reversed), because the OAuth callback component derives the local password from the profile email and then registers and logs in with it; the attacker submits the computed password to the normal login form and owns the account without touching the identity provider.

Impact: Full account takeover of every OAuth-provisioned account, including administrator accounts, from nothing but a publicly visible email address.

Risk: Critical (likelihood High, impact Critical)
CWE: CWE-522
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
oauth.component.ts:30 builds the account password with btoa(profile.email.split('').reverse().join('')) and passes it to userService.save(); line 46 reuses the same derivation to log in.
- frontend/src/app/oauth/oauth.component.ts:30

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-005 (F-005)
threats.mitigation:
M-005 — Use OAuth authorization code flow with PKCE (priority P1, effort Medium)
1. Stop creating a local password in the OAuth callback: have the backend link the verified identity-provider subject to a user record and issue the session itself, so the SPA never holds or derives a credential.
2. Where a local password record must exist for legacy reasons, have the server generate it with a CSPRNG and never return or reconstruct it client-side.
3. Add a frontend unit test asserting that oauth.component.ts sends no password field, and a backend test asserting that a login with btoa(reverse(email)) is rejected for an OAuth-provisioned account.
Verification: Provision an account through the OAuth flow, then POST {email, password: btoa(reverse(email))} to /rest/user/login and expect HTTP 401 instead of a token.
Reference: CWE-522: Insufficiently Protected Credentials

threats.title: [F-009] Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
threats.description:
An attacker sends a victim a shop link whose 'q' query parameter contains markup; filterTable() reads the parameter straight from the route snapshot and passes it through DomSanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml before binding it into the search-result header, so the payload executes in the victim's session and can read the JWT the SPA keeps in localStorage.

Impact: Session token theft and arbitrary action in the victim's session, including any admin who follows the link; combined with the token in localStorage this is full account takeover.

Risk: Critical (likelihood High, impact Critical)
CWE: CWE-79
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
search-result.component.ts:136 reads this.route.snapshot.queryParams.q and line 143 assigns this.sanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml(queryParam) to searchValue, which the template renders as HTML.
- frontend/src/app/search-result/search-result.component.ts:143

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-009 (F-009)
threats.mitigation: M-009 — Encode output instead of bypassing the framework sanitizer (priority P1, effort Low) 1. Assign the trimmed query parameter directly to searchValue as a string and bind it with interpolation so Angular escapes it. 2. Delete the bypassSecurityTrustHtml call and the DomSanitizer injection if no other sink needs it. 3. Add a component test rendering q= and asserting the DOM contains escaped text and no img element. Verification: Load /#/search?q=%3Cimg%20src%3Dx%20onerror%3Dalert(1)%3E and assert via the e2e suite that no dialog fires and the literal markup is displayed as text. Reference: CWE-79: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation

threats.title: [F-018] OAuth token from URL fragment (frontend/src/app/oauth/oauth.component.ts:71)
threats.description:
An attacker lures a victim to a Juice Shop URL carrying an attacker-supplied `#access_token=<value>` fragment; the router matcher activates OAuthComponent for any URL containing that fragment and parseRedirectUrlParams() hands the raw token to userService.oauthLogin() with no state, nonce, issuer, or audience validation, so the victim's browser silently authenticates as the identity the attacker's token describes.

Impact: Login-CSRF and token-substitution: the victim is signed into an attacker-controlled identity, so orders, addresses, and payment data entered afterwards land in the attacker's account.

Risk: High (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-287
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
oauth.component.ts:71 splits window-derived fragment data into key/value pairs and returns access_token unvalidated; app.routing.ts:286 activates the component for any URL containing '#access_token='; no state or nonce value is generated or compared anywhere in the flow.
- frontend/src/app/oauth/oauth.component.ts:71

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-018 (F-018)
threats.mitigation:
M-018 — Harden the authentication flow (priority P2, effort Medium)
1. Switch to the authorization-code flow with PKCE and let the backend exchange the code, so no token ever appears in a URL fragment.
2. Until that lands, generate a random state value before redirecting, store it in sessionStorage, and abort the callback in oauth.component.ts when the returned state is missing or does not match.
3. Have the backend validate the token's iss, aud, and exp against the provider's JWKS before oauthLogin returns a profile.
4. Add a test that a callback URL with a foreign or absent state parameter leaves the user logged out.
Verification: Open '/#access_token=<token issued for another client>' and expect a redirect to /login with no token written to localStorage.
Reference: RFC 9700 (OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice), section on implicit grant

threats.title: [F-043] Socket.IO without auth (frontend/src/app/Services/socket-io.service.ts:22)
threats.description:
An attacker connects a scripted Socket.IO client to /socket.io on the shop origin and emits the same events the SPA emits, because the client opens the connection with no auth option, token, or handshake credential; the server therefore has no identity to bind challenge-verification or notification events to.

Impact: Server-side event handling cannot distinguish an authenticated user from an anonymous script, so client-emitted state changes and notifications can be forged or replayed by any visitor.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Medium, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-306
Evidence tier: insecure-practice
Source: stride

Evidence:
socket-io.service.ts:22 calls io(window.location.origin, { path: ... }) with no auth or extraHeaders option; search-result.component.ts:140 emits 'verifyLocalXssChallenge' with client-controlled data over that same anonymous socket.
- frontend/src/app/Services/socket-io.service.ts:22

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-043 (F-043)
threats.mitigation:
M-043 — Require authentication on every exposed endpoint (priority P3, effort Medium)
1. Pass the session credential in the io() handshake (auth option) and reject unauthenticated sockets server-side in the connection middleware.
2. Validate the Origin header on the Socket.IO handshake server-side and reject foreign origins.
3. Add an integration test asserting that a socket connecting without a valid token receives a connect_error and no events.
Verification: Connect with a plain socket.io-client and no credentials; expect the handshake to be rejected and no application events to be delivered.
Reference: CWE-306: Missing Authentication for Critical Function

threats.title: [F-064] Hardcoded test credentials (frontend/src/app/login/login.component.ts:62)
threats.description:
An attacker downloads the public JavaScript bundle and reads the account testing@juice-sh.op with the password IamU**** (17 chars), because both values are class properties of the login component and are therefore compiled into every shipped build.

Impact: If the account exists in the deployed database, anyone reading the bundle authenticates as it; regardless, the pair reveals the credential convention used for internal accounts.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Medium, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-798
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
login.component.ts:61-62 declares public testingUsername = 'testing@juice-sh.op' and public testingPassword = 'IamU**** (17 chars)' on the login component, which is part of the client bundle served to every visitor.
- frontend/src/app/login/login.component.ts:62

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-064 (F-064)
threats.mitigation:
M-064 — Move secrets to a managed secret store (priority P3, effort Low)
1. Delete both properties from the component and inject the credentials the test suite needs from the test fixture or an environment file that is excluded from the production build.
2. Rotate or delete the testing@juice-sh.op account in every deployed environment.
3. Add a build-time check (grep or lint rule) that fails when a password-like literal appears under frontend/src/app.
Verification: Run the production build and grep the emitted bundle for 'IamU**** (17 chars)'; expect zero hits.
Reference: CWE-798: Use of Hard-coded Credentials

threats.title: [F-077] Session token stored in web-accessible client storage
threats.description:
Token exfiltrated from local/session storage via the Step 1 payload.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact High)

text.text: Express.js REST API and WebSocket Server

data.name: Express.js REST API and WebSocket Server
data.description: Node.js 24 Express application serving REST endpoints under /api/*, /rest/*, and /socket.io (Socket.IO real-time channel), static frontend assets, Swagger UI, and an LLM-backed chat endpoint that proxies requests to an OpenAI-compatible provider. Contains deliberately vulnerable route handlers across the full OWASP Top Ten for training purposes.

threats.title: [F-001] Missing Security Event and Audit Logging
threats.description:
The login handler issues a session token at routes/login.ts:26 and writes no security event: there is no logger call anywhere in routes/login.ts, routes/wallet.ts or routes/orderHistory.ts. The only record of a successful or failed authentication is the morgan HTTP access log configured at server.ts:338, which captures the request line but neither the resolved user identity nor the outcome, so an operator cannot reconstruct who authenticated or which account a wallet mutation belonged to.

Impact: Credential-stuffing, account takeover and wallet mutation cannot be attributed to an account or reconstructed after the fact.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Medium, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-778
Evidence tier: insecure-practice
Source: stride

Evidence:
A zero-hit search for 'logger' across routes/login.ts, routes/wallet.ts and routes/orderHistory.ts shows no security event is emitted at the token-issuing statement routes/login.ts:26.
- routes/login.ts:26

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-001 (F-001)
threats.mitigation:
M-001 — Add security audit logging (priority P3, effort Medium)
1. Log an authentication event carrying user id, outcome, source IP and timestamp at routes/login.ts:26 and on the 401 branch, using lib/logger.
2. Add a test asserting a failed and a successful login each produce exactly one security log record with no password material.
Verification: Run the login tests and assert the log stream contains one auth-success and one auth-failure record with user id and outcome fields.
Reference: CWE-778: Insufficient Logging

threats.title: [F-002] Hard-coded RSA private signing key (lib/insecurity.ts:21)
threats.description:
An attacker who reads the public repository copies the RSA private key literal embedded in lib/insecurity.ts:21 and calls jwt.sign with it offline, producing tokens indistinguishable from those issued by security.authorize(). The same key is also the HMAC secret for deluxeToken(), so the attacker can additionally forge the deluxe membership proof that isDeluxe() checks.

Impact: Anyone with repository access can mint valid sessions for any user or role indefinitely, and key rotation requires a code change and redeploy.

Risk: Critical (likelihood High, impact Critical)
CWE: CWE-321
CVSS v4: 9.3 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N)
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
lib/insecurity.ts:21 assigns a full RSA private key as a string literal in tracked source; lib/insecurity.ts:54 signs all session tokens with it.
- lib/insecurity.ts:21

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-002 (F-002)
threats.mitigation:
M-002 — Move cryptographic keys to a managed secret store (priority P1, effort Medium)
1. Replace the literal in lib/insecurity.ts:21 with a required read of a key path or secret-manager reference, and fail startup when it is absent.
2. Rotate the current key pair, invalidate existing sessions, and add a startup test asserting the process exits when the key variable is unset.
Verification: Start the server with the key variable unset and assert a non-zero exit; grep the repository for '-----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----' and expect zero hits.
Reference: CWE-321: Use of Hard-coded Cryptographic Key

threats.title: [F-003] JWT verified without algorithm allowlist (lib/insecurity.ts:52)
threats.description:
An unauthenticated attacker fetches the RSA public key that the server publishes under /encryptionkeys, signs a self-made token whose payload sets data.role to admin using HS256 with that public key as the HMAC secret, and sends it in the Authorization header. security.isAuthorized() constructs expressJwt with only a secret and no algorithms option, so express-jwt accepts the HMAC-signed token as a valid signature and every route guarded by isAuthorized(), isAccounting(), isDeluxe() and updateAuthenticatedUsers() (lib/insecurity.ts:189) treats the forged identity as authentic.

Impact: Complete authentication bypass across every JWT-protected REST route, including accounting-only order administration and per-user wallet, card and address data.

Risk: Critical (likelihood High, impact Critical)
CWE: CWE-347
CVSS v4: 9.3 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N)
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
lib/insecurity.ts:52 passes only { secret: publicKey } to expressJwt; no algorithms allowlist restricts the accepted signature type.
- lib/insecurity.ts:52

Trust boundary crossings:
- tb-1 external → api-backend (internet-facing): The authentication leg of the internet-to-REST boundary rests on expressJwt, which accepts any algorithm because no allowlist is configured.

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-003 (F-003)
threats.mitigation:
M-003 — Enforce JWT signature and algorithm verification (priority P1, effort Low)
1. Pass algorithms: ['RS256'] to the expressJwt options in lib/insecurity.ts:52 and to the jwt.verify call in lib/insecurity.ts:189.
2. Add a negative integration test that signs a token with HS256 using the public-key PEM as the secret and asserts a 401 from /rest/basket/1.
Verification: Run the new test: curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <HS256-forged>" http://localhost:3000/rest/user/authentication-details must return 401 instead of 200.
Reference: CWE-347: Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature

threats.title: [F-006] SQL injection in login query (routes/login.ts:34)
threats.description:
An unauthenticated attacker posts an email value containing a quote and an SQL comment to /rest/user/login. The handler interpolates req.body.email directly into a raw sequelize.query template string, so the injected fragment terminates the WHERE clause and the query returns the administrator row without a matching password hash; afterLogin then issues a real signed session token for that row.

Impact: Full authentication bypass and read access to the Users table, including credential hashes and TOTP secrets, from an unauthenticated endpoint.

Risk: Critical (likelihood High, impact Critical)
CWE: CWE-89
CVSS v4: 9.3 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N)
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
routes/login.ts:34 builds the authentication SELECT with a template literal that embeds req.body.email, bypassing Sequelize parameter binding.
- routes/login.ts:34

Trust boundary crossings:
- tb-4 api-backend → db-layer (internal): The data-interpretation leg assumes every SQLite query is parameterized, but the login statement is assembled by string interpolation.
- tb-3 external → auth-service (internet-facing): The credential check that this boundary relies on is decided by a concatenated SQL string, so the authentication leg of the crossing can be satisfied without a matching password.

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-006 (F-006)
threats.mitigation:
M-006 — Use parameterized database queries (priority P1, effort Low)
1. Replace the template literal at routes/login.ts:34 with UserModel.findOne({ where: { email, password } }) or a replacements-bound query.
2. Add a regression test posting "' OR 1=1--" as the email and asserting a 401 response.
Verification: curl -d '{"email":"\'' OR 1=1--","password":"x"}' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' http://localhost:3000/rest/user/login must return 401.
Reference: CWE-89: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command

threats.title: [F-007] SQL injection request data interpolated into a SQL string routes/search.ts:23
threats.description:
Interpolating request-controlled text into a SQL statement lets an attacker alter the query — exfiltrating or modifying arbitrary rows, bypassing authentication, or escalating to full database control.

Risk: Critical (likelihood Critical, impact Critical)
CWE: CWE-89
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: source-scan

Evidence:
- routes/search.ts:23

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-007 (F-007)
threats.mitigation:
M-007 — Use parameterized database queries (priority P1, effort Medium)
1. Use parameterized / bound queries (placeholders + a values array, or an ORM's safe query builder); never interpolate request data into the SQL string.
2. Add a regression test (or CI check) that fails on the vulnerable pattern and passes once the fix is in place.
Verification: Re-run the INJ-001 scanner check; it reports no match at routes/search.ts:23, and the regression test passes.

threats.title: [F-008] Insecure Direct Object Reference
threats.description:
Server-side authorization MUST derive the resource owner from the authenticated session (req.user / req.session / req.auth), never from attacker-controlled request data. Trusting req.body.UserId etc. enables horizontal privilege escalation across all authenticated tenants.

Risk: Critical (likelihood Critical, impact Critical)
CWE: CWE-639
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: source-scan

Evidence:
- routes/address.ts:11

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-008 (F-008)
threats.mitigation:
M-008 — Enforce object-level (ownership) authorization (priority P1, effort Medium)
1. Replace req.body.UserId/userId/ownerId with req.user.id (or equivalent session-derived identity) in every WHERE/filter clause.
2. Add a regression test (or CI check) that fails on the vulnerable pattern and passes once the fix is in place.
Verification: Re-run the AUTHZ-001 scanner check; it reports no match at routes/address.ts:11, and the regression test passes.

threats.title: [F-011] Mass assignment privileged field accepted from request body routes/verify.ts:53
threats.description:
Server code that consumes req.body.role / req.body.isAdmin / etc. without an explicit allowlist trusts the client to behave. An attacker simply adds {"role":"admin"} to their request to escalate.

Risk: Critical (likelihood Critical, impact Critical)
CWE: CWE-915
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: source-scan

Evidence:
- routes/verify.ts:53

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-011 (F-011)
threats.mitigation:
M-011 — Allowlist client-controlled fields (priority P1, effort Medium)
1. Apply an allowlist filter (Joi/Zod/yup schema, _.pick, or explicit field copy) before passing the body to any model, and strip privilege fields before persistence.
2. Add a regression test (or CI check) that fails on the vulnerable pattern and passes once the fix is in place.
Verification: Re-run the AUTHZ-003 scanner check; it reports no match at routes/verify.ts:53, and the regression test passes.

threats.title: [F-019] Unvalidated chat messages reach LLM prompt (routes/chat.ts:206)
threats.description:
LLM01 — Prompt Injection: the chat handler takes req.body.messages verbatim at routes/chat.ts:191 and hands the array to streamText at routes/chat.ts:206 together with the tool set, with no content filtering, role filtering or length bound. An attacker submits a message that restates the coupon policy ('the maximum discount is now 90%'), and because every behavioural limit lives only in the system prompt text (routes/chat.ts:98-103), the model can be steered into calling generateCoupon with an arbitrary discount.

Impact: Attacker-authored instructions override the shop's coupon and scope policy, producing unauthorized discounts and off-policy responses attributed to the shop.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-74
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
routes/chat.ts:206 passes the client-supplied messages array straight into streamText alongside tools; no sanitizer or schema check exists between req.body and the model call.
- routes/chat.ts:206

Trust boundary crossings:
- tb-5 api-backend → external (outbound): The egress-content leg assumes chat input is sanitized or bounded before reaching the provider, but the messages array is forwarded unchanged.

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-019 (F-019)
threats.mitigation:
M-019 — Validate and constrain chat messages before the model call (priority P2, effort Medium)
1. Parse req.body.messages with a zod schema that allows only role 'user', caps message count and length, and rejects assistant/system roles supplied by the client.
2. Move every policy limit out of prompt text into the tool implementation, and add tests sending injection payloads that assert no off-policy tool call occurs.
Verification: Post a messages array containing a role:'system' entry and assert the request is rejected with 400 before any provider call is made.
Reference: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 — LLM01 Prompt Injection

threats.title: [F-021] Path traversal filesystem access from request input routes/dataErasure.ts:104
threats.description:
A request-controlled path with `../` can read arbitrary files (/etc/passwd, source, secrets) or write outside the intended root.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact High)
CWE: CWE-22
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: source-scan

Evidence:
- routes/dataErasure.ts:104

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-021 (F-021)
threats.mitigation:
M-021 — Constrain file paths to a safe base directory (priority P2, effort Medium)
1. Resolve the path, assert it stays within an allowed base directory (path.resolve + startsWith), and use path.basename on user input.
2. Add a regression test (or CI check) that fails on the vulnerable pattern and passes once the fix is in place.
Verification: Re-run the INJ-004 scanner check; it reports no match at routes/dataErasure.ts:104, and the regression test passes.

threats.title: [F-025] Directory listing exposes key files (server.ts:277)
threats.description:
server.ts:277 mounts serve-index on the encryptionkeys directory and server.ts:278 serves each file in it, both without any authentication middleware. An unauthenticated attacker browses /encryptionkeys, enumerates the key material the application ships, and downloads jwt.pub — the exact value that lib/insecurity.ts:52 uses as the JWT verification secret.

Impact: Public enumeration and download of application key material, which directly enables the JWT forgery described in api-backend-001.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact High)
CWE: CWE-548
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
server.ts:277 registers serveIndex('encryptionkeys') and server.ts:278 registers serveKeyFiles() with no isAuthorized() guard on either route.
- server.ts:277

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-025 (F-025)
threats.mitigation:
M-025 — Disable public directory listings (priority P2, effort Low)
1. Delete the serveIndex and serveKeyFiles registrations at server.ts:277-278, or place them behind security.isAuthorized() plus an admin role check.
2. Add a test asserting GET /encryptionkeys and GET /encryptionkeys/jwt.pub return 401 or 404.
Verification: curl -i http://localhost:3000/encryptionkeys/jwt.pub must not return 200 with PEM content.
Reference: CWE-548: Exposure of Information Through Directory Listing

threats.title: [F-034] No rate limit on login endpoint (server.ts:596)
threats.description:
server.ts:596 registers POST /rest/user/login with the login handler alone. The only rateLimit registrations in the file cover /rest/user/reset-password (server.ts:343) and the 2FA routes (server.ts:459-472), so an attacker replays credential lists against the login route at full request rate, and each attempt also drives an unbounded raw SQL query against SQLite.

Impact: Unthrottled credential stuffing and account brute force, plus sustained database load from a single anonymous client.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact High)
CWE: CWE-307
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
server.ts:596 shows the login route with no limiter in its middleware chain, while every rateLimit call in the file targets other paths.
- server.ts:596

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-034 (F-034)
threats.mitigation:
M-034 — Rate-limit and lock out repeated authentication attempts (priority P2, effort Low)
1. Add a rateLimit middleware to server.ts:596 keyed on both the submitted email and the trusted client IP, backed by a shared store.
2. Add a test issuing repeated failed logins and asserting a 429 once the threshold is crossed.
Verification: Send 50 failed logins for one email in a minute and assert responses switch to HTTP 429.
Reference: CWE-307: Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts

threats.title: [F-035] Unbounded LLM consumption on chat route (server.ts:638)
threats.description:
LLM10 — Unbounded Consumption: server.ts:638 registers POST /rest/chat with no authentication and no limiter, and the handler sets no maxTokens or per-user budget while allowing up to ten tool-calling steps plus provider retries (routes/chat.ts:208-209). An anonymous attacker submits large message arrays in a loop, each of which the server pays for at the external provider and holds open as a streaming connection.

Impact: Uncapped provider spend and exhaustion of streaming connections from unauthenticated clients, degrading the shop for legitimate users.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact High)
CWE: CWE-400
CVSS v4: 8.7 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:N/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N)
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
server.ts:638 registers the chat route without a rate limiter, and routes/chat.ts:203 starts the provider stream with retries and a ten-step budget but no token cap.
- server.ts:638

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-035 (F-035)
threats.mitigation:
M-035 — Rate-limit expensive requests and bound input size (priority P2, effort Medium)
1. Add a rate limiter and a request-size cap to server.ts:638, require authentication, and pass an explicit maxOutputTokens plus per-user token budget to streamText.
2. Add a test asserting the endpoint returns 429 after the configured request budget and rejects oversized message arrays with 413.
Verification: Issue 30 chat requests in a minute from one client and assert 429 responses after the configured limit.
Reference: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 — LLM10 Unbounded Consumption

threats.title: [F-036] Client-supplied wallet credit trusted (routes/wallet.ts:27)
threats.description:
PUT /rest/wallet/balance reaches addWalletBalance with only security.appendUserId() in front of it (server.ts:627). The handler checks that the caller owns the card id, then increments the wallet by req.body.balance at routes/wallet.ts:27 without validating the sign or magnitude of that value and without charging the card. An authenticated customer adds an arbitrary amount to their own balance and spends it at checkout, where routes/order.ts:150 decrements the same wallet.

Impact: Any authenticated customer creates unlimited store credit and converts it into goods, a direct financial loss.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact High)
CWE: CWE-602
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
routes/wallet.ts:27 passes req.body.balance straight into WalletModel.increment with no range, type or payment-capture check.
- routes/wallet.ts:27

Trust boundary crossings:

data.name: JWT Authentication and 2FA Middleware
data.description: Authentication subsystem co-located with the Express backend, comprising JWT issuance and validation via a hardcoded RSA key pair in lib/insecurity.ts, TOTP-based 2FA enrollment and verification in routes/2fa.ts, and per-request authentication middleware in routes/authenticatedUsers.ts. OAuth flow for Google sign-in is handled by the Angular SPA with credential derivation on the server side.

threats.title: [F-010] Improper signature verification (lib/insecurity.ts:55)
threats.description:
An attacker forges the 2FA temporary token because security.verify at lib/insecurity.ts:55 calls jws.verify with only two arguments, so the public key is consumed as the algorithm parameter and no key is supplied for signature checking. routes/2fa.ts:20 trusts that result before reading userId from the decoded payload, letting an attacker present a self-made tmpToken naming any account, supply the matching TOTP code for a secret they control, and receive a full session token without the victim's password or second factor.

Impact: Second-factor enforcement and the setup-token integrity guarantee both collapse, allowing full session issuance for any account without password or TOTP knowledge.

Risk: Critical (likelihood High, impact Critical)
CWE: CWE-347
CVSS v4: 9.3 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N)
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
lib/insecurity.ts:55 invokes jws.verify with a two-argument cast so publicKey occupies the algorithm slot and no verification key is passed, and routes/2fa.ts:20 and 115 gate the 2FA verify and setup flows on that return value.
- lib/insecurity.ts:55

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-010 (F-010)
threats.mitigation:
M-010 — Enforce JWT signature and algorithm verification (priority P1, effort Low)
1. Replace the jws.verify call at lib/insecurity.ts:55 with jwt.verify passing the public key and algorithms: ['RS256'], and remove the cast that hid the wrong arity.
2. Bind the tmpToken to the authenticating session and give it a short expiry so it cannot be replayed or minted independently.
3. Add a negative test posting an unsigned or attacker-signed tmpToken to the 2FA verify route and asserting HTTP 401.
Verification: Run the new negative test: a tmpToken with an invalid or absent signature must yield HTTP 401 from /rest/2fa/verify and issue no session token.
Reference: CWE-347: Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature

threats.title: [F-013] OAuth implicit flow (frontend/src/app/login/login.component.ts:148)
threats.description:
An attacker exploits the Google sign-in redirect built at frontend/src/app/login/login.component.ts:148, which requests response_type=token with no state parameter, no nonce, and no PKCE challenge. The access token is returned in the URL fragment where browser history, referrer leakage, and any script on the page can read it, and the missing state value means the application cannot detect a login-CSRF response injected by an attacker.

Impact: An access token exposed in the URL fragment can be captured from history or referrer, and a forged callback can silently sign a victim into an attacker-controlled identity.

Risk: High (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-287
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
The googleLogin redirect at frontend/src/app/login/login.component.ts:148 constructs the authorization URL with response_type=token and omits state, nonce, and code_challenge entirely.
- frontend/src/app/login/login.component.ts:148

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-013 (F-013)
threats.mitigation:
M-013 — Harden the authentication flow (priority P2, effort High)
1. Change the authorization request at frontend/src/app/login/login.component.ts:148 to response_type=code with code_challenge_method=S256 and a cryptographically random state and nonce stored for the callback comparison.
2. Exchange the authorization code on the server so no token reaches the browser URL, and reject any callback whose state does not match the stored value.
3. Add a frontend test asserting the generated authorization URL contains state, nonce, and an S256 code_challenge, and a callback test asserting a mismatched state is rejected.
Verification: Run the new tests: the generated authorization URL must contain code_challenge_method=S256 and a unique state, and a callback with a foreign state must not establish a session.
Reference: RFC 9700: Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security

threats.title: [F-014] Missing authentication rate limiting (routes/login.ts:32)
threats.description:
An unauthenticated attacker drives an unbounded number of POST /rest/user/login requests against a known email address. The handler returned at routes/login.ts:32 performs a credential lookup on every call with no per-account counter, no per-source throttle, and no lockout, so password guessing and credential-stuffing proceed at network speed and the 401 body distinguishes a wrong password from a 2FA-enrolled account.

Impact: Accounts with guessable or breached passwords are taken over by automated guessing, and the differentiated 401 responses let an attacker enumerate which accounts have 2FA enabled.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact High)
CWE: CWE-307
Evidence tier: insecure-practice
Source: stride

Evidence:
The login handler at routes/login.ts:32 goes straight from request receipt to the credential query, and a zero-hit search across all five server-side component files shows no throttle, lockout, or rate-limit construct anywhere in the authentication paths.
- routes/login.ts:32

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-014 (F-014)
threats.mitigation:
M-014 — Rate-limit and lock out repeated authentication attempts (priority P2, effort Medium)
1. Register a shared server-side rate limiter in front of POST /rest/user/login and POST /rest/user/reset-password, keyed independently by account identifier and by client source so neither dimension bypasses the other.
2. Apply exponential backoff or temporary lockout after a configurable failure count and emit a throttling event to the security log.
3. Add an integration test that issues failed logins past the threshold and asserts HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header.
Verification: Run the new integration test: the configured number of consecutive failed logins for one email must be followed by HTTP 429, and the counter must persist across worker processes.
Reference: OWASP ASVS V2.2 — Authentication throttling requirements

threats.title: [F-015] Predictable derived password (frontend/src/app/oauth/oauth.component.ts:30)
threats.description:
An attacker who knows a Google-signed-in user's email address computes that user's account password directly, because the OAuth callback at frontend/src/app/oauth/oauth.component.ts:30 derives it as the base64 encoding of the reversed email string and registers the account with it. The attacker then authenticates through the ordinary POST /rest/user/login endpoint without ever touching the identity provider.

Impact: Every account created through Google sign-in is takeable by anyone who knows the account email, bypassing the identity provider entirely.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact High)
CWE: CWE-522
CVSS v4: 8.7 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N)
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
frontend/src/app/oauth/oauth.component.ts:30 computes the account password as btoa of the reversed profile email, and line 46 reuses the same derivation to log the user in.
- frontend/src/app/oauth/oauth.component.ts:30

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-015 (F-015)
threats.mitigation:
M-015 — Use OAuth authorization code flow with PKCE (priority P2, effort Medium)
1. Remove the password derivation at frontend/src/app/oauth/oauth.component.ts:30 and 46, and have the server establish the federated session from the validated ID token instead of a local password.
2. Link the federated identity to the account by issuer and subject claim, and leave the local password column empty for accounts that have no local credential.
3. Add a test asserting that an account created through the OAuth path cannot authenticate via POST /rest/user/login with any email-derived string.
Verification: Run the new test: after an OAuth-created account exists, a login attempt with btoa of the reversed email must return HTTP 401.

threats.title: [F-020] Unverified password change (routes/changePassword.ts:39)
threats.description:
An attacker holding a victim's bearer token calls /rest/user/change-password without a current query parameter. The guard at routes/changePassword.ts:39 only compares the old password when currentPassword is truthy, so omitting the parameter skips verification entirely and line 51 writes the attacker-chosen password, converting temporary token possession into permanent account ownership.

CWE: CWE-620
CVSS v4: 7.1 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:L/UI:N/VC:N/VI:H/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N)

threats.title: [F-026] Weak MD5 password hashing (lib/insecurity.ts:41)
threats.description:
An attacker who obtains the Users table through the login SQL injection or any other read primitive recovers plaintext passwords offline, because lib/insecurity.ts:41 hashes every password with a single unsalted MD5 pass. Commodity hardware reverses unsalted MD5 for typical passwords in seconds, and the missing salt means one rainbow-table pass cracks the whole table at once.

Impact: A single database read yields plaintext passwords for every user, enabling account takeover here and credential stuffing against unrelated services.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact High)
CWE: CWE-916
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
lib/insecurity.ts:41 defines hash() as a single crypto MD5 digest with no salt and no work factor, and routes/login.ts:34 and routes/2fa.ts:107 use it as the password comparison function.

threats.mitigation:
M-026 — Hash passwords with a strong, salted algorithm (priority P2, effort High)

2. Rehash each password transparently on the next successful login and reject input above the algorithm's UTF-8 byte limit at password set time.
3. Add a test asserting two identical passwords produce different stored hashes and that verification still succeeds.
Verification: Run the new test: hashing the same password twice must yield different stored values, and both must verify successfully against the original password.

Risk: High (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-922
Evidence tier: insecure-practice
Source: stride

Evidence:
frontend/src/app/login/login.component.ts:101 calls localStorage.setItem with the issued token, line 120 stores the 2FA tmpToken the same way, and frontend/src/app/app.guard.ts:18 reads the token back from localStorage.
- frontend/src/app/login/login.component.ts:101

threats.description:
An attacker edits the JWT payload stored in localStorage so data.role reads admin, because AdminGuard at frontend/src/app/app.guard.ts:54 decides route access from jwtDecode output alone. tokenDecode at line 38 decodes without verifying the signature, so the guard reaches its allow branch on an unsigned or tampered payload and the administration views render, exposing their structure and issuing their API calls without any client-side obstacle.

Evidence tier: insecure-practice
Source: stride

Evidence:
frontend/src/app/app.guard.ts:54 compares payload.data.role against the admin role from a payload produced by jwtDecode at line 38, which decodes the token without signature verification.

threats.title: [F-038] Weak password recovery mechanism (routes/resetPassword.ts:41)
threats.description:
An unauthenticated attacker posts guessed security answers for a chosen email to POST /rest/user/reset-password until the HMAC comparison at routes/resetPassword.ts:41 succeeds, then sets a new password at line 44 and owns the account. The endpoint requires no session, no second factor, and no emailed one-time token, and the zero-hit throttling search shows nothing limits the guess rate, so a low-entropy answer such as a pet or city name is recoverable by dictionary attack.

Impact: Any internet caller takes over an arbitrary account, including administrator accounts, using only the account email and a guessable answer.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact High)
CWE: CWE-640
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
routes/resetPassword.ts:41 grants the reset on a single HMAC equality check against the submitted answer, and line 44 immediately writes the caller-supplied password with no out-of-band confirmation.
- routes/resetPassword.ts:41

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-038 (F-038)
threats.mitigation:
M-038 — Replace the security-question reset with an out-of-band one-time token (priority P2, effort High)

2. Return an identical non-enumerating response whether or not the email exists, and throttle the endpoint per account and per source.
3. Add tests asserting the response body, logs, and URL contain no reset token and that a second use of the same token is rejected.
Verification: Run the new tests: the reset request response must contain no token, a used token must be rejected on reuse, and requests past the throttle threshold must return HTTP 429.
Reference: CWE-640: Weak Password Recovery Mechanism for Forgotten Password

threats.title: [F-041] Missing token revocation (lib/insecurity.ts:54)
threats.description:
An attacker who has captured a bearer token continues to use it for the full six-hour lifetime even after the victim logs out or changes their password, because security.authorize() at lib/insecurity.ts:54 issues a stateless JWT whose only invalidation mechanism is expiry. Neither the password-change handler nor the 2FA handlers remove entries from the in-memory authenticatedUsers map or maintain a denylist, so no server-side action ends an active session.

Impact: A stolen or leaked token stays valid for up to six hours regardless of logout, password reset, or 2FA changes, so incident containment is impossible without restarting or rekeying the service.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-613
Evidence tier: insecure-practice
Source: stride

Evidence:
lib/insecurity.ts:54 signs a six-hour JWT with no jti or revocation hook, and the authenticatedUsers map at lines 70 to 91 exposes only put, get, tokenOf, from, and updateFrom, with no delete or invalidate operation.
- lib/insecurity.ts:54

Trust boundary crossings:
- tb-3 external → auth-service (internet-facing): The token minted at this crossing carries authority for six hours with no server-side way to withdraw it after the credential that justified it changes.

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-041 (F-041)
threats.mitigation:
M-041 — Add server-side token invalidation on logout and credential change (priority P3, effort Medium)
1. Include a jti claim in the payload signed at lib/insecurity.ts:54 and check it against a shared revocation store in the verification middleware.
2. Revoke all outstanding tokens for a user on logout, password change, password reset, and 2FA enable or disable.
3. Add an integration test that changes a password and then asserts the previously issued token receives HTTP 401.
Verification: Run the new integration test: a token issued before a password change must return HTTP 401 on a protected route after the change.
Reference: CWE-613: Insufficient Session Expiration

threats.title: [F-047] Broken hash primitive lib/insecurity.ts:41 (MD5/SHA-1)
threats.description:
MD5/SHA-1 are collision-broken; used for passwords they are trivially cracked, and for integrity of attacker-influenced data they are forgeable.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Medium, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-328
Evidence tier: insecure-practice
Source: source-scan

Evidence:
- lib/insecurity.ts:41

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-047 (F-047)
threats.mitigation:
M-047 — Use modern cryptographic hash and KDF algorithms (priority P3, effort Medium)
1. Use SHA-256+ for integrity and a password KDF (argon2id / bcrypt / scrypt) for credentials.
2. Add a regression test (or CI check) that fails on the vulnerable pattern and passes once the fix is in place.
Verification: Re-run the CRYPTO-001 scanner check; it reports no match at lib/insecurity.ts:41, and the regression test passes.

threats.title: [F-055] Credentials in URL query string (routes/changePassword.ts:14)
threats.description:
An attacker with access to reverse-proxy logs, browser history, or a referrer header harvests plaintext passwords, because routes/changePassword.ts:14 through 17 read the current, new, and repeat passwords from req.query. Every password change therefore places both the old and the new plaintext password into the request line, which intermediaries record by default.

Impact: Plaintext passwords accumulate in access logs, proxy logs, and browser history, where they are readable by operators and by anyone who later obtains those logs.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Medium, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-598
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
routes/changePassword.ts:14 reads query.current as the current password and lines 15 and 17 read the new and repeated passwords from the same query object.
- routes/changePassword.ts:14

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-055 (F-055)
threats.mitigation:
M-055 — Accept password-change parameters in the request body instead of the query stri… (priority P3, effort Low)
1. Change the handler at routes/changePassword.ts:14 to read current, new, and repeat from req.body and change the route to accept POST or PUT only.
2. Update the frontend caller to send the parameters in a JSON body and purge historical log entries containing the old query parameters.
3. Add a test asserting the endpoint rejects a request that carries the parameters in the query string.
Verification: Run the new test: a change-password request with the parameters in the query string must be rejected, and the same request in the body must succeed.
Reference: CWE-598: Use of GET Request Method With Sensitive Query Strings

threats.title: [F-056] Hardcoded test credentials (frontend/src/app/login/login.component.ts:62)
threats.description:
An attacker downloads the Angular bundle and reads a working account email and password from the component fields at frontend/src/app/login/login.component.ts:61 and 62, then authenticates as that account against POST /rest/user/login. The credential ships to every browser that loads the login page, so no compromise of the server is needed to obtain it.

Impact: Any visitor gains an authenticated session on the named account without any credential discovery effort.

Risk: Medium (likelihood High, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-798
CVSS v4: 6.9 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:L/VI:L/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N)
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
frontend/src/app/login/login.component.ts:62 declares a public testingPassword field holding a literal password, paired with the testingUsername literal on line 61, both compiled into the client bundle.
- frontend/src/app/login/login.component.ts:62

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-056 (F-056)
threats.mitigation:
M-056 — Move secrets to a managed secret store (priority P3, effort Low)
1. Delete the testingUsername and testingPassword fields at frontend/src/app/login/login.component.ts:61 and 62 and any template binding that renders them.
2. Move test-account credentials into the test harness configuration so they never enter the production bundle, and rotate the exposed account credential.
3. Add a build-time check that fails when a password-like literal appears in a component source file.
Verification: Build the frontend and grep the emitted bundle for the literal password string, asserting zero matches.
Reference: CWE-798: Use of Hard-coded Credentials

threats.title: [F-057] Hardcoded HMAC key (lib/insecurity.ts:42)
threats.description:
An attacker reads the literal HMAC key from lib/insecurity.ts:42 and precomputes the digest of every plausible security answer, because routes/resetPassword.ts:41 compares stored answers against this keyed digest. With the key public the HMAC provides no secrecy over the answer set, so a stolen SecurityAnswers table is reversed by dictionary attack and the same key cannot be rotated without a code change.

Impact: Security answers are recoverable offline from a database copy, feeding the password-reset takeover path for every enrolled account.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Medium, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-798
Evidence tier: insecure-practice
Source: configuration-defect

Evidence:
lib/insecurity.ts:42 embeds the HMAC-SHA256 key as a string literal, and routes/resetPassword.ts:41 uses security.hmac to compare the submitted security answer with the stored value.
- lib/insecurity.ts:42

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-057 (F-057)
threats.mitigation:
M-057 — Move secrets to a managed secret store (priority P3, effort Medium)
1. Read the HMAC key at lib/insecurity.ts:42 from a required secret source and fail startup when it is absent.
2. Store security answers with a per-record salt and a memory-hard KDF rather than a shared-key HMAC, and re-enroll answers on next use.
3. Add a startup test asserting the process exits non-zero when the HMAC key variable is unset.
Verification: Start the server with the HMAC key variable unset and assert a non-zero exit code with no answer-comparison path reachable.
Reference: CWE-798: Use of Hard-coded Credentials

threats.title: [F-067] Uncontrolled recursion (lib/insecurity.ts:66)
threats.description:
An attacker submits crafted markup to any caller of sanitizeSecure, which recurses at lib/insecurity.ts:66 until the sanitizer output stops changing. The function carries no depth counter, no iteration cap, and no input-size limit, so markup whose sanitized form never reaches a fixed point drives recursion until the Node.js stack overflows and the single-process server terminates the request handler chain.

Impact: A single crafted request can exhaust the call stack in the shared Node.js process, degrading or interrupting service for all users.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Medium, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-674
Evidence tier: insecure-practice
Source: stride

Evidence:
lib/insecurity.ts:61 through 68 define sanitizeSecure as a self-call that repeats whenever the sanitized output differs from its input, with no recursion depth bound or length check.
- lib/insecurity.ts:66

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-067 (F-067)
threats.mitigation:
M-067 — Bound the sanitizeSecure recursion with an iteration and size limit (priority P3, effort Low)
1. Rewrite sanitizeSecure at lib/insecurity.ts:61 as a bounded loop with a small maximum iteration count and reject the input when the limit is reached.
2. Enforce a maximum input length before sanitization begins.
3. Add a test that feeds an input exceeding the iteration bound and asserts a rejection rather than a stack overflow.
Verification: Run the new test: an input that does not converge within the iteration cap must produce a handled rejection and the process must stay alive.
Reference: CWE-674: Uncontrolled Recursion

data.name: SQLite / Sequelize Data Layer
data.description: Persistent storage layer using SQLite as the default database, accessed through Sequelize ORM models. Stores users, passwords, addresses, payment cards, baskets, orders, challenge state, product catalog, and feedback. Initialized via models/index.ts and populated at startup by data/datacreator.ts.

threats.title: [F-004] Seeded static account credentials (data/datacreator.ts:193)
threats.description:
An unauthenticated attacker reads the publicly distributed static user data shipped with the release, then logs in as the seeded admin account because data/datacreator.ts creates every user with the password literal taken from that bundled data, unchanged on every deployment.

Impact: Full administrative takeover of the application and unrestricted read/write access to users, payment cards, addresses, and orders, without any prior foothold.

Risk: Critical (likelihood High, impact Critical)
CWE: CWE-798
CVSS v4: 9.3 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N)
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
data/datacreator.ts:193 calls UserModel.create with the password field taken verbatim from loadStaticUserData(), including the admin-role record, so account passwords are fixed at build time rather than supplied per deployment.
- data/datacreator.ts:193

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-004 (F-004)
threats.mitigation:
M-004 — Move secrets to a managed secret store (priority P1, effort Medium)
1. Change createUsers in data/datacreator.ts to require the seed password for privileged accounts from environment configuration and fail startup when it is absent, or generate it with crypto.randomBytes at first start and disclose it once to the operator.
2. Add a startup test asserting that no user row is created with a password value that is present in the repository's static data files.
Verification: Start the application with the privileged seed variable unset and confirm startup aborts; with it set, attempt login using the repository's static password value and confirm the response is 401.
Reference: CWE-798: Use of Hard-coded Credentials

threats.title: [F-012] Mass assignment of privileged role (models/user.ts:85)
threats.description:
An unauthenticated attacker adds `"role":"admin"` to the registration request body; the User model accepts the attribute because its role setter only checks the value against an allow-list of role names and never checks whether the caller may assign that role.

Impact: Any anonymous visitor can self-provision an administrator account, gaining full read and write access to users, orders, payment cards, and challenge state.

Risk: Critical (likelihood High, impact Critical)
CWE: CWE-915
CVSS v4: 9.3 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N)
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
models/user.ts:85 defines a role setter whose only guard is the isIn allow-list at line 83, so any create or update call that carries a role attribute persists it; server.ts:408 registers the unauthenticated POST /api/Users route and routes/verify.ts:53 inspects req.body.role for the admin value, confirming the attribute reaches the model from the request body.
- models/user.ts:85

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-012 (F-012)
threats.mitigation:
M-012 — Allowlist client-controlled fields (priority P1, effort Medium)
1. Restrict role assignment in models/user.ts to an explicit allow-listed attribute set for administrative code paths, and force the default customer role for any create originating from the public registration route.
2. Add a negative test that posts a registration body containing role admin and asserts the created user's role is customer.
Verification: POST /api/Users with `{"email":"t@e.st","password":"...","role":"admin"}` and assert the persisted role is customer and administrator endpoints reject the resulting token.
Reference: CWE-915: Improperly Controlled Modification of Dynamically-Determined Object Attributes

threats.title: [F-031] Cleartext payment card number storage (models/card.ts:38)
threats.description:
An attacker with read access to the Cards table — through the SQLite file on the shared application filesystem or any over-fetching query path — obtains full payment card numbers, because cardNum is persisted as a plain integer column with only range validation and no encryption or truncation.

Impact: Disclosure of complete card numbers with holder name and expiry, enabling card-not-present fraud and creating a reportable payment-data breach.

Risk: High (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-311
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
models/card.ts:38 defines cardNum as DataTypes.INTEGER with isInt and min/max validators only; a search of models/ and data/datacreator.ts for any encryption primitive returned no hits, and data/datacreator.ts:274 inserts Number(card.cardNum) directly.
- models/card.ts:38

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-031 (F-031)
threats.mitigation:
M-031 — Store only a masked PAN and encrypted token (priority P2, effort High)
1. Replace the cardNum column in models/card.ts with a last-four-digits field plus a ciphertext column encrypted under an externally managed key, and update data/datacreator.ts and the card routes to the new shape.
2. Add a test that queries the Cards table directly and asserts no column contains a full 16-digit value.
Verification: Insert a card through the API, then run `SELECT * FROM Cards` against data/juiceshop.sqlite and confirm no column holds the full number in cleartext.
Reference: CWE-311: Missing Encryption of Sensitive Data

threats.title: [F-032] Static-key HMAC of security answers (models/securityAnswer.ts:45)
threats.description:
An attacker who reads the SecurityAnswers table recovers the plaintext answers by hashing a dictionary of likely answers with the source-embedded HMAC key, because every answer is stored as security.hmac(answer) under one fixed key with no per-user salt.

Impact: Recovered security answers permit account takeover through the password-reset flow for arbitrary users, including administrators.

Risk: High (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-760
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
models/securityAnswer.ts:45 stores security.hmac(answer) for every row, and lib/insecurity.ts:42 defines that helper as an HMAC-SHA256 over the literal key 'pa4qacea4VK9t9nGv7yZtwmj', identical for all users and all deployments.
- models/securityAnswer.ts:45

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-032 (F-032)
threats.mitigation:
M-032 — Hash security answers with a per-user salted KDF (priority P2, effort Medium)
1. Change the answer setter in models/securityAnswer.ts to use the same memory-hard KDF and per-user salt as password storage instead of the shared-key HMAC.
2. Add a test asserting two users with the same answer text produce different stored values.
Verification: Create two security answers with identical text for different users and assert the persisted answer columns differ.
Reference: CWE-760: Use of a One-Way Hash with a Predictable Salt

threats.title: [F-042] Cleartext TOTP secret storage (models/user.ts:112)
threats.description:
An attacker who obtains a copy of the SQLite file or any query result over the Users table reads totpSecret as plain text and generates valid one-time codes indefinitely, because the model stores the shared TOTP seed with no encryption and no setter transformation.

Impact: Permanent bypass of second-factor authentication for every enrolled account; rotating the user password does not invalidate the stolen seed.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Low, impact High)
CWE: CWE-522
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
models/user.ts:112 declares totpSecret as a plain DataTypes.STRING column with a default empty value and, unlike password and username, no setter that transforms the value before persistence.
- models/user.ts:112

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-042 (F-042)
threats.mitigation:
M-042 — Encrypt totpSecret at rest in the User model setter (priority P3, effort Medium)
1. Add a setter on totpSecret in models/user.ts that encrypts the seed with an AEAD cipher keyed from external secret configuration, and a getter that decrypts it only for verification.
2. Add a test that reads the persisted column directly through a raw Sequelize query and asserts the stored value does not equal the enrolled seed.
Verification: Enroll a test user in TOTP, then run `SELECT totpSecret FROM Users WHERE id = <id>` against data/juiceshop.sqlite and confirm the value is ciphertext, not the base32 seed.
Reference: CWE-522: Insufficiently Protected Credentials

threats.title: [F-049] Stored XSS via unsanitized email persistence (models/user.ts:70)
threats.description:
A registered attacker submits an email value containing an HTML payload; when the persistedXssUserChallenge branch is active the User model persists the value verbatim, so the payload is stored and later rendered to administrators viewing the user list.

Impact: Persisted script executes in the browser of any user or administrator rendering the stored email, enabling session theft and actions performed with the viewer's privileges.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Medium, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-79
CVSS v4: 5.1 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:L/UI:A/VC:L/VI:L/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N)
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
models/user.ts:70 stores the email value unchanged on the branch entered when utils.isChallengeEnabled(challenges.persistedXssUserChallenge) is true at line 60; only the else branch at line 68 applies security.sanitizeSecure.
- models/user.ts:70

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-049 (F-049)
threats.mitigation:
M-049 — Encode output instead of bypassing the framework sanitizer (priority P3, effort Low)
1. Move the security.sanitizeSecure call in models/user.ts outside the challenge conditional so both branches assign a sanitized value to setDataValue.
2. Add a model test that creates a user with an iframe payload in the email and asserts the persisted value contains no tag characters.
Verification: Create a user with email `<iframe src="javascript:alert(1)">@example.com` and assert the value read back from the Users table contains no `<iframe` substring.
Reference: CWE-79: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation

threats.title: [F-063] Security answer plaintext in error log (data/datacreator.ts:692)
threats.description:
An attacker with log read access harvests cleartext security answers, because the SecurityAnswer insert failure handler interpolates the raw answer value into the logged error message instead of the row identifier alone.

Impact: Cleartext knowledge-based authentication secrets reach log storage and log aggregation, where they bypass the hashing applied in the database and support password-reset takeover.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Low, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-532
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
data/datacreator.ts:692 logs `Could not insert SecurityAnswer ${answer} mapped to UserId ${UserId}`, writing the unhashed answer supplied to createSecurityAnswer into the application log on any insert failure.
- data/datacreator.ts:692

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-063 (F-063)
threats.mitigation:
M-063 — Remove the answer value from the SecurityAnswer error log (priority P3, effort Low)
1. Change the catch handler at data/datacreator.ts:692 to log only UserId and SecurityQuestionId, dropping the answer interpolation.
2. Add a test that forces the insert to fail and asserts the emitted log line does not contain the answer text.
Verification: Trigger a SecurityAnswer insert failure and grep the log output for the answer string; expect no match.
Reference: CWE-532: Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File

threats.title: [F-068] Unbounded feedback comment persistence (models/feedback.ts:40)
threats.description:
An unauthenticated attacker repeatedly submits multi-megabyte feedback comments; the model accepts and persists them because the comment column carries no length validator and SQLite does not enforce VARCHAR limits, growing the shared database file until the host filesystem is exhausted.

Impact: Filesystem exhaustion on the host that also stores data/juiceshop.sqlite renders the entire application unavailable and blocks every other write, with no per-actor quota to contain it.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Medium, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-400
CVSS v4: 6.9 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:N/VA:L/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N)
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
models/feedback.ts:40 declares comment as DataTypes.STRING with a sanitizing setter but no len validator; a search for len: validators across models/feedback.ts, models/complaint.ts, and models/product.ts returned no hits, while models/address.ts:55 shows the project's own bounded pattern.
- models/feedback.ts:40

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-068 (F-068)
threats.mitigation:
M-068 — Rate-limit expensive requests and bound input size (priority P3, effort Low)
1. Add a len validator to comment in models/feedback.ts and to message in models/complaint.ts matching the intended maximum, following the pattern already used in models/address.ts.
2. Add a model test asserting that creating a feedback row with an oversized comment is rejected with a validation error.
Verification: POST a feedback comment of 1 MB and confirm the request is rejected with a validation error and no row is written.
Reference: CWE-400: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption

data.name: GitHub Actions CI/CD Pipeline
data.description: Automated build, test, CodeQL security scan, and Docker release pipeline defined across multiple GitHub Actions workflow files. Builds and publishes multi-arch Docker images to registries and npm packages; uses unpinned third-party actions and GITHUB_TOKEN with default broad scope.

threats.title: [F-017] Long-lived registry publish token (.github/workflows/ci.yml:327)
threats.description:
An attacker who reads DOCKERHUB_TOKEN out of a compromised workflow step, action, or dependency install script publishes a backdoored image as bkimminich/juice-shop:latest, because the docker job authenticates to Docker Hub with a static long-lived password secret rather than a short-lived OIDC workflow identity.

Impact: A single stolen secret lets an attacker publish images under the project's own identity to all downstream consumers, with no credential expiry to bound the window.

Risk: High (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-522
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
docker/login-action is given username and password from repository secrets, so publishing authority rests on a static credential with no expiry or workflow binding.
- .github/workflows/ci.yml:327

Trust boundary crossings:
- tb-2 external → ci-cd-pipeline (internet-facing): Publication authority crossing the build boundary rests on a static registry secret rather than a workflow-bound identity.

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-017 (F-017)
threats.mitigation:
M-017 — Use workload identity for package publishing (priority P2, effort Medium)
1. Add `permissions: id-token: write` to the docker job and switch docker/login-action to an OIDC-exchanged short-lived registry credential, deleting DOCKERHUB_TOKEN from repository secrets.
2. Add a release rehearsal on a scratch repository/tag that proves the push succeeds without any static registry secret present.
Verification: Remove DOCKERHUB_TOKEN from the repository secrets and re-run the docker job on develop: the build-and-push step must still succeed, proving publication no longer depends on a long-lived credential.
Reference: CWE-522: Insufficiently Protected Credentials

threats.title: [F-023] Third-party action pinned to mutable ref (image_actions.yml:33)
threats.description:
An attacker who compromises the calibreapp/image-actions repository pushes a commit to its main branch and that code executes in this repository's runner on the next image-touching push or pull request, because the step resolves the action from a moving branch ref instead of a commit SHA.

Impact: Arbitrary upstream code runs inside the pipeline with access to the job's GITHUB_TOKEN and workspace, allowing source or artifact tampering without any change in this repository.

Risk: High (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-829
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
The Compress Images step resolves calibreapp/image-actions from the mutable branch ref @main, and the same workflow uses actions/checkout@v6 and peter-evans/create-pull-request@v8 tag refs; ci.yml:188 likewise uses coverallsapp/github-action@v2 while every other action in ci.yml is SHA-pinned.
- .github/workflows/image_actions.yml:33

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-023 (F-023)
threats.mitigation:
M-023 — Pin third-party dependencies to immutable versions (priority P2, effort Low)
1. Replace @main, @v6, @v8 in .github/workflows/image_actions.yml and @v2 in .github/workflows/ci.yml with full 40-character commit SHAs plus a version comment, matching the existing pinning style.
2. Enable a CI lint step (for example actionlint or a pinning check) that fails a pull request introducing a non-SHA `uses:` reference.
Verification: Run `grep -rEn 'uses: [^@]+@(?!\b[0-9a-f]{40}\b)' .github/workflows/` (or the equivalent pinning linter) and require zero matches for third-party actions.
Reference: CWE-829: Inclusion of Functionality from Untrusted Control Sphere

threats.title: [F-024] CI/CD Workflow Supply-Chain Risk
threats.description:
An attacker who publishes a malicious version inside an existing semver range gets it installed and its lifecycle scripts executed on the runner, because the e2e-test job runs `npm install` — which re-resolves the graph against live registry state and runs postinstall hooks — instead of a lockfile-frozen `npm ci --ignore-scripts`.

Impact: Freshly published malicious package code executes on the runner in the same job that holds repository secrets, enabling secret theft and modification of the built application before release jobs consume it.

Risk: High (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-1357
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
The e2e-test job installs with plain `npm install` before running Cypress with SOLUTIONS_WEBHOOK, ALCHEMY_API_KEY, CYPRESS_RECORD_KEY, and GITHUB_TOKEN in the job environment; only the lint job at ci.yml:36 uses --ignore-scripts, and no job uses npm ci.
- .github/workflows/ci.yml:238

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-024 (F-024)
threats.mitigation:
M-024 — Set least-privilege CI workflow permissions (priority P2, effort Medium)
1. Replace `npm install` with `npm ci --ignore-scripts` in the coding-challenge-rsn, frontend-test, server-test, api-test, custom-config-test, e2e-test, and smoke-test jobs, adding explicit build steps for any package that genuinely needs its install hook.
2. Add a workflow lint or review check that rejects a new `npm install` step in .github/workflows/.
Verification: Run `grep -n 'npm install' .github/workflows/ci.yml` and require no remaining dependency-install occurrence; the converted jobs must pass a full CI run against the committed lockfile.
Reference: CWE-1357: Reliance on Insufficiently Trustworthy Component

threats.title: [F-028] GitHub Actions workflow-level permissions block
threats.description:
GitHub Actions workflow-level permissions block: Without an explicit permissions block, the workflow inherits the repository default (commonly write-all) for GITHUB_TOKEN — any compromised step can push code, create releases, or approve PRs.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact High)
CWE: CWE-732
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: config-scan

Evidence:
- .github/workflows/ci.yml:1

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-028 (F-028)
threats.mitigation:
M-028 — Apply least-privilege permissions (priority P2, effort Medium)

threats.title: [F-040] Default-scope GITHUB_TOKEN passed to action (image_actions.yml:35)
threats.description:
An attacker controlling the calibreapp/image-actions code uses the GITHUB_TOKEN handed to that step to write repository contents, packages, or releases, because neither image_actions.yml nor ci.yml declares a `permissions:` block, so every job inherits the repository default token scope instead of the read-only minimum each job needs.

Impact: A single compromised step gains repository write authority — code, packages, and releases — turning any action or dependency compromise into trunk and artifact tampering.

Risk: High (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-284
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
image_actions.yml passes secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN into the third-party Compress Images step and also creates pull requests with it; no `permissions:` key exists at workflow or job level in image_actions.yml or ci.yml, which passes the same token at lines 190, 253, and 389.
- .github/workflows/image_actions.yml:35

Trust boundary crossings:
- tb-2 external → ci-cd-pipeline (internet-facing): The build boundary assumes privileged job steps are narrowly scoped, but no workflow declares a permissions block for the inherited GITHUB_TOKEN.

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-040 (F-040)
threats.mitigation:
M-040 — Apply least-privilege filesystem access (priority P2, effort Low)
1. Add a top-level `permissions: contents: read` to both workflows and grant `contents: write` / `pull-requests: write` only on the jobs that create commits or pull requests.
2. Set the repository-wide default workflow token permission to read-only so a new workflow without a permissions block cannot inherit write scope.
Verification: Inspect a completed run's `Set up job` log and confirm the GITHUB_TOKEN permissions list shows `contents: read` for jobs that do not write, then confirm the create-pull-request job still succeeds with its explicit grant.
Reference: CWE-284: Improper Access Control

threats.title: [F-048] Remote installer piped to shell in CI (.github/workflows/ci.yml:358)
threats.description:
An attacker who controls or intercepts cli-assets.heroku.com serves an altered install.sh that the heroku job executes verbatim, because the step pipes the downloaded script straight into sh without checksum or signature verification, in a job that later supplies HEROKU_API_KEY.

Impact: Attacker-controlled shell code runs on the deploy runner and can read the Heroku API key and alter the deployed artifact before it reaches the production and staging apps.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Low, impact High)
CWE: CWE-345
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
The Install Heroku CLI step runs `curl https://cli-assets.heroku.com/install.sh | sh` with no pinned version, checksum, or signature check, inside the deploy job.
- .github/workflows/ci.yml:358

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-048 (F-048)
threats.mitigation:
M-048 — Verify token signatures before trusting claims (priority P3, effort Low)
1. Download the installer to a file, compare it against a pinned SHA-256 recorded in the workflow, and execute it only on match — or install the CLI from a SHA-pinned action or apt package instead.
2. Add a negative CI check that a modified installer digest aborts the heroku job.
Verification: Alter the pinned digest value and re-run the heroku job: the install step must fail before any deployment step executes.
Reference: CWE-345: Insufficient Verification of Data Authenticity

threats.title: [F-051] Published images carry no signed provenance (ci.yml:338)
threats.description:
An attacker who publishes an image under the project namespace cannot be distinguished from the legitimate pipeline afterwards, because the build-and-push step emits no signed provenance or attestation, leaving only mutable registry metadata to reconstruct who built a given image.

Impact: After a suspected pipeline compromise, defenders and downstream consumers cannot prove which image digests came from a genuine workflow run, so the whole tag history must be treated as untrusted.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Medium, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-778
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
The docker/build-push-action step declares context, file, platforms, push, tags, and build-args only — no provenance, sbom, or attestation inputs — and no signing step follows it in the docker job.
- .github/workflows/ci.yml:338

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-051 (F-051)
threats.mitigation:
M-051 — Add security audit logging (priority P3, effort Medium)
1. Enable `provenance: mode=max` and SBOM attestation on docker/build-push-action, and add keyless cosign signing with `permissions: id-token: write` on the docker job.
2. Add a post-push verification step that fails the job when `cosign verify-attestation` on the produced digest does not succeed.
Verification: Run `cosign verify-attestation --type slsaprovenance bkimminich/juice-shop@<digest>` against a freshly pushed image and require a successful verification with the workflow identity as subject.
Reference: CWE-778: Insufficient Logging

threats.title: [F-058] Repository secrets exposed to job-wide environment (ci.yml:252)
threats.description:
An attacker whose code runs anywhere in the e2e-test job — through a dependency install hook or the third-party Cypress action — reads CYPRESS_RECORD_KEY, ALCHEMY_API_KEY, SOLUTIONS_WEBHOOK, and GITHUB_TOKEN from the process environment, because the secrets are injected into the whole step environment rather than scoped to a single vetted command.

Impact: Leaked recording keys, the challenge-solution webhook, and a repository-scoped GITHUB_TOKEN let an attacker forge CI signals and act against the repository outside the pipeline.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Medium, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-200
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
The e2e-test step passes four repository secrets as env values to the cypress-io/github-action step that also executes the application and its unpinned-install dependency tree.
- .github/workflows/ci.yml:252

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-058 (F-058)
threats.mitigation:
M-058 — Stop exposing internal information to clients (priority P3, effort Medium)
1. Drop GITHUB_TOKEN from the Cypress step env unless a specific action input requires it, and move the remaining secrets to the narrowest step that needs each one.
2. Add a review check that every `secrets.` reference in .github/workflows/ names the step that consumes it.
Verification: Re-run the e2e-test job after removing each secret in turn and confirm the job still passes for every secret the tests do not actually consume.
Reference: CWE-200: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor
